header.question:
A document in the library contains this sentence:

> Using individual neurons as these units has had some success (Olah et al., 2020; Bills et al., 2023), but a key challenge has been that neurons are often polysemantic, activating for several unrelated types of feature (Olah et al., 2020).

Check what the sentence says about the work it cites against that work in the library. Does the cited source support it? Cite the page(s) of the cited source that show what it actually says.

events.delta:
Verdict: supported

The sentence makes two claims about Olah et al. (2020), which is *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits*. The library supports both. It also says one thing the sentence leaves out.

**Neurons as units have had some success.**
- Olah et al. say that "thousands of hours of studying individual neurons have led us to believe the typical case is that neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22).
- The same paragraph gives examples of meaningful features, such as early-layer edge or curve detectors and later-layer wheel detectors (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22).
- It also notes that "the community is divided on whether this is true" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22). So "some success" is a fair, modest summary.

**Neurons are often polysemantic.**
- The source says: "Neural networks often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs." Its example is an InceptionV1 neuron that responds to cat faces, fronts of cars, and cat legs (distill:zoom-in/r1/b62).
- The paper stresses that the neuron isn't tracking a hidden shared feature. Feature visualization shows it looking for "the eyes and whiskers of a cat, for furry legs, and for shiny fronts of cars" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b64). That matches "several unrelated types of feature."
- It calls polysemantic neurons "a major challenge for the circuits agenda, significantly limiting our ability to reason about neural networks" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b65). That matches "a key challenge."

**Limits of this check.**
- Olah et al. also say such features can still be studied: "We can still study such features, characterizing each different case they fire, and reason about their circuits to some extent" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b65). The challenge is real but not fatal in their view.
- I did not check the other citation, Bills et al. (2023), *Language models can explain neurons in language models*. The library only has it as a reference-list entry in another paper (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p10), not as a document. I can't confirm what it says about neuron-level success.
